title: EPPO Arrests Suspect in $79M Cross-Border VAT Fraud Probe
content:
The European Public Prosecutor’s Office has arrested another suspect in its “Escape Room” investigation into a cross-border VAT carousel fraud network operating across six EU countries. 

The wider network allegedly used hundreds of shell companies and fictitious invoices to conceal transactions involving electronic devices and evade VAT in Austria, Belgium, Germany, Latvia, the Netherlands and Poland. EPPO estimates the scheme caused at least $79 million in losses in the Netherlands and Belgium. Eight other suspects were arrested in Belgium, the Netherlands and Poland in October 2025. 

Prosecutors allege the arrested man acted as a broker between companies in the scheme, improperly claimed VAT refunds and continued the operation through new companies after authorities raided the network in 2025. His activities alone may have caused about $4.6 million in losses, while authorities seized around $4 million in real estate, a car, stock, receivables and bank accounts.
snippet: The European Public Prosecutor’s Office has arrested another suspect in its “Escape Room” investigation into a cross-border VAT carousel fraud network operating across six EU countries.

title: Human Trafficking Raid Exposes Suspected Cyber Scam Operation in Papua New Guinea
content:
Papua New Guinea police rescued 39 Indonesians believed to have been trafficked to work in a cyber scam compound, the first case of its kind uncovered in the Pacific island nation.

Four Chinese nationals were also detained in connection with the Tuesday raid in the country’s capital, Port Moresby, PNG police Commissioner David Manning told OCCRP.

“What we did find in there was 39 Indonesian citizens, 34 that were male and five females, all adults but they’ve been in very cramped, very cramped conditions,” Manning said.

Manning also said police seized a large number of documents and electronic devices from the property, a house in Port Moresby’s inner suburbs. He said the incident was the first case he was aware of involving the suspected trafficking of foreign nationals into the country to carry out online fraud.

He added that as far as he is aware Papua New Guinea was the final destination for the suspected trafficking victims.

“All indications are they were brought in specifically to run this scam from Papua New Guinea,” he said.

title: Former Mother-In-Law of Dismissed Ukraine Prosecutor General Denies Buying Dubai Villa
content:
With a cloud of controversy hanging over former Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko — who was dismissed last week after his office was raided by anti-corruption officers — information has now emerged about a mystery villa in Dubai.

Records show Kravchenko’s former mother in law was listed as the owner of the Dubai villa. But she denies making the purchase.

Alina Shkrobanets acquired villa for about $670,000 in 2023, according to leaked Dubai property data obtained by OCCRP and shared with Schemes, the investigative unit of RFE/RL’s Ukrainian Service.

At the time, Kravchenko headed the Kyiv Regional Military Administration and was married to Alina Shkrobanets' daughter, Olena.

“I didn’t buy anything in the United Arab Emirates,” Alina Shkrobanets told Schemes, suggesting her identity details might have been used without her knowledge.

“I’m wondering if someone might have used my information against me,” she said in a phone interview.

title: Albanian Court Orders House Arrest for Intelligence Chief
content:
An Albanian court has ordered the director of the State Intelligence Service (SHISH), Vlora Hyseni, to be put under house arrest and suspended from public duty as part of a sweeping investigation into public tender fraud, the Special Prosecutor’s Office (SPAK) announced Tuesday. The development prompted Prime Minister Edi Rama to announce her immediate removal from office.

The Special Court against Corruption and Organized Crime (GJKKO) approved the security measures at the request of SPAK. Prosecutors are investigating Hyseni for allegedly assisting a perpetrator of a criminal offense and disclosing state secrets.

However, the house arrest order could not be immediately executed because Hyseni was in Baku, Azerbaijan, attending an international conference of intelligence service heads when officers searched her apartment.

Speaking from New York, Prime Minister Edi Rama said Hyseni’s dismissal is immediate and that he will consult President Bajram Begaj to appoint a successor, emphasizing that the court must determine her guilt or innocence independently.

title: Romanian Ex-Presidential Candidate Held in €1.1M Fraud Case
content:
Romanian prosecutors have asked a Bucharest court to place former presidential candidate Călin Georgescu and businessman Ionel Rusen in pretrial detention for 30 days over an alleged organized criminal group and a 1.1 million euro ($1.26 million) fraud. 

According to a prosecution filing reviewed by OCCRP, investigators allege Georgescu, Rusen and Italian businessman Massimiliano Arena persuaded a Romanian businessman to transfer money as a guarantee for a foreign credit line that never materialized. Prosecutors say Georgescu initiated the arrangement and introduced Rusen as someone capable of securing the financing.

The victim first transferred 1 million euros and later another 100,000 euros after being told the loan could be increased from six million euros to 15 million, the filing says. Prosecutors detained Georgescu and Rusen for 24 hours following searches that uncovered electronic devices, signal jammers and documents suspected of being false. The filing also cites secretly recorded conversations in which Georgescu discussed buying property in Italy and seeking political asylum, which prosecutors cited in arguing that he posed a flight risk.

title: Disappearance of 2 Journalists in Djibouti Raises Concerns for Their Safety
content:
The Committee to Protect Journalists said Sunday that it is “deeply concerned” by reports that South African investigative journalist Micah Reddy and local fixer Kooki Mahmoud have gone missing in Djibouti, and urged authorities “to immediately clarify their whereabouts and ensure their safety.”

Contact with Reddy, the African coordinator for the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ), and Mahmoud, a Djibouti-based journalist, was lost Saturday at approximately 1 p.m. local time, said an ICIJ statement. The statement, issued Sunday, said ICIJ is gravely concerned for their safety and authorities in Djibouti have not so far responded to its requests for information.

“We are calling on the government of Djibouti to: Immediately clarify Reddy and Mahmoud's whereabouts and confirm their well-being; Launch a prompt, transparent investigation into their disappearance; Keep their families, colleagues and employers fully and promptly informed,” the ICIJ statement said.

title: Bosnia Seizes 1.1 Tons of Synthetic Drugs Worth Up to €33 Million
content:
Authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina have seized nearly 1.1 metric tonnes of dangerous synthetic cathinones with a potential street value of up to 33 million euros ($37.82 million), and arrested two suspects, marking the largest synthetic drug bust in the history of the nation of roughly 3.5 million people, the State Border Service announced.

The seized substance—an extremely dangerous stimulant used as a substitute for cocaine and ecstasy—carries a wholesale market value of 5 million euros ($5.73 million), but its street value skyrockets when broken down into individual grams sold at 20 to 30 euros ($23 to $34.50) each across the region, according to the Border Police. In addition to the massive drug cache, officers confiscated a firearm, mobile phones, corporate documentation, official stamps, and specialized full-face respirator masks with advanced air-filtration systems used to protect operators during chemical synthesis and drug "cooking." The Border Police noted that investigators have not yet established the origin or final destination of the shipment, as the investigation remains ongoing.

title: Iraq Sentences Former Electricity Director General to Seven Years for illicit enrichment
content:
An Iraqi anti-corruption court has sentenced the former director general of a state electricity distribution firm to seven years in prison for illicit enrichment, ordering him to forfeit nearly $20 million in restitution and fines as part of a sweeping crackdown on graft in the country’s power sector.

The official, Alaa Samir Rashid Shukr Al-Jubouri, who headed the state-owned General Company of Electricity Distribution (Middle Region), was convicted by Iraq’s Central Criminal Court for Combating Corruption. According to the country’s Integrity Commission, Rashid amassed unexplained wealth exceeding 5.5 billion Iraqi dinars (about $4.2 million) along with an additional $5.5 million in U.S. currency.

The court ordered Rashid to return the illicit gains and levied an equivalent fine, bringing his total financial liability to approximately $19.4 million. Judges also upheld a freeze on his movable and immovable assets, paving the way for seizure.

title: Georgia Court Sentences Ex-Security Chief to 13 Years in Prison in Corruption Case
content:
The former head of the State Security Service of Georgia was found guilty this week of accepting more than $2 million in bribes and sentenced to 13 years in prison, as a corruption crackdown continues against former senior officials from the ruling Georgian Dream party. 

Grigol Liluashvili, who headed the security service from 2019 until 2025, was arrested last December following raids on his home and those of two other former ruling party elites.

Tbilisi City Court Judge Nino Tarashvili on Wednesday found Liluashvili guilty of “accepting bribes on an especially large scale,” said the Prosecutor's Office of Georgia’s press release announcing the verdict. 

Liluashvili’s lawyer Lana Tsertsvadze reacted outside the courtroom, telling reporters it was an “unjust verdict” that she would appeal.

“The defense and Mr. Grigol Liluashvili anticipated an acquittal because there was not a single piece of evidence in the case to prove his guilt,” Tsertsvadze said in a video interview. “Mr. Grigol Liluashvili will seek to establish his innocence through legal avenues. This unfounded, unlawful, and unjust decision will be challenged in the Court of Appeals.”
snippet: The former head of the State Security Service of Georgia was found guilty this week of accepting more than $2 million in bribes and sentenced to 13 years in prison, as a corruption crackdown continues

title: Six Convicted, €300M Confiscation Ordered in Mafia-Linked EU Tax Fraud
content:
A Milan court has sentenced six individuals to prison and ordered the confiscation of more than 300 million euros ($344.66 million) for their roles in a transnational tax fraud and money laundering syndicate tied to the Italian mafia, the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) announced on Thursday.

The convictions mark the latest judicial actions in "Operation Moby Dick," a massive EPPO investigation into a VAT carousel fraud scheme. Between 2020 and 2023, the network issued over 1.3 billion euros ($1.49 billion) in fake invoices for AirPods, laptops, and other electronics, resulting in 520 million euros ($597.35 million) in losses to EU and national budgets.

The Milan judge confirmed aggravated circumstances for the criminal syndicate’s aiding and abetting of a mafia association. According to the EPPO, one of the convicted defendants received illicit funds from a Camorra clan—which investigators previously linked to the Nuvoletta and Di Lauro groups—and funneled the money into the scheme to launder the mafia's proceeds.

title: Former Maduro Ally Pleads Guilty in US to $195M Money Laundering Scheme
content:
A Miami federal court brought a decade of investigative reporting to a close on Wednesday as Colombian-born businessman Alex Saab pleaded guilty to money laundering—years after Venezuelan news outlet Armando.info first began uncovering his state corruption schemes.

Saab, a top financial ally of ousted Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro, admitted to using the U.S. financial system to launder bribes connected to Venezuela’s Local Committees for Supply and Production (CLAP)—a state program meant to distribute food to impoverished communities. He faces up to 20 years in federal prison and has agreed to forfeit $195 million, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.

The guilty plea serves as a vindication for Armando.info, a local investigative news outlet and OCCRP member center. More than  nine years ago, the outlet pioneered reporting that brought Saab out of the shadows, exposing his ties to multimillion-dollar state contracts and the delivery of low-quality food to vulnerable populations.

At the time, Saab and the Maduro government vehemently denied the links. Saab sued the Armando.info team in Venezuela, arguing he had no connection to the CLAP program.

title: Belgian Court Rules Treasury Lacked Authority to Reject Release of Russian Assets
content:
Belgium’s supreme administrative court has ruled that a decision by the country’s treasury department refusing to release frozen Russian assets was illegal.

The court, known as the Council of State, ruled that the Administrator General of the Treasury lacked the proper legal competence to determine whether or not to release the assets.

The September 11 ruling was first reported by De Tijd on Wednesday, and shared with OCCRP. 

The case originates from a request submitted by Russia’s BCS Bank in January 2023 to unfreeze its securities and cash, which had been blocked at Brussels-based securities manager Euroclear. 

The assets were frozen following E.U. sanctions imposed in 2022 on Moscow's main securities holder, the National Settlement Depository, in response to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In July 2024, the Belgian treasury rejected BCS Bank’s request to unfreeze its securities and cash. The treasury alleged that the lender had failed to prove it had fully severed ties with Russia’s National Settlement Depository.

The Council of State ruling does not necessarily mean the frozen funds will be released.

title: Hackers Demand $3M Ransom in Revolut Data Leak
content:
A group claiming responsibility for a recent Revolut data breach has demanded 6,000 Monero—an untraceable, privacy-focused cryptocurrency—worth about $3 million, threatening to sell sensitive information belonging to hundreds of the fintech company’s customers if it is not paid within 24 hours.

The group, calling itself “iamnotavillain,” posted the ultimatum on its website on Wednesday alongside a countdown clock. It threatened to sell the information to other criminal groups if Revolut failed to pay.

A Revolut spokesperson told Reuters late Wednesday that the company had received no direct contact or ransom demand from the people claiming responsibility for the breach, and that there had been no negotiations with them.

The company first confirmed the breach on September 12, saying an unauthorized party had submitted fraudulent requests for customer information using an email account on the legitimate domain of a government agency. Revolut said its own systems and customer funds were not compromised and that it blocked the address after discovering the fraud.

title: Citizen Lab: Israeli Firm May Have Run Angola Influence Campaign
content:
Israeli influence-for-hire company BlackCore appears to have trained members of an Angolan government communications team and helped them run a covert social media campaign, according to research by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab.

Citizen Lab examined websites and other online infrastructure linked to BlackCore and obtained what researchers identified as the company’s final report on a training program in Angola. One BlackCore webpage, titled “Angolan Government Campaign,” advertised training in storytelling, copywriting, traffic management and social media operations. It also described plans to launch live campaigns on Meta and TikTok.

The final report said the program began on January 19, 2026, and continued for more than 14 weeks, ending sometime in April. BlackCore described the goal as replacing what it called “amateur production practices” with a “professional, robust, and scalable Architecture for State communications.”

According to the report, participants produced more than 40 pieces of content, while trainers evaluated at least 24 publications. Materials reviewed by Citizen Lab also showed Facebook and Instagram accounts and pages used in the campaign.

title: Thousands Protest in Malta After Businessman Acquitted in Journalist's Murder
content:
Outrage spilled onto the streets of the Maltese capital on Wednesday evening as demonstrators gathered at the heart of Valletta, shifting from vigils to protests to demand political accountability following the acquittal of the alleged mastermind behind the 2017 assassination of investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.

For 107 consecutive months - on the 16th of every month since Caruana Galizia was killed by a car bomb outside her home - civil society groups held silent vigils. But the Sept. 2 acquittal of Yorgen Fenech, a prominent businessman accused of orchestrating and financing the plot, transformed that quiet grief into open defiance.

Chanting “Mafia! Mafia!” and “Injustice!”, thousands of protesters marched from the Parliament building to a memorial standing directly opposite Malta’s Law Courts to lay flowers and light candles before Caruana Galizia’s portrait. Banners carried by the crowd called for the protection of journalists and democracy, declaring: “The Trial Has Ended. Our Work Has Not” and “Impunity Ends Here.”

title: French Prosecutors Seek Up to 5 Years in Prison for Sons of Ex-Yemeni President Saleh Over Ill-Gotten Assets
content:
Two sons of late Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh could face up to five years in prison as a Paris court hears charges against them for allegedly laundering tens of millions of euros in embezzled state funds and corruption proceeds.

The trial, which opened September 7 at the Paris Criminal Court, follows a 2019 investigation launched by France's National Financial Prosecutor's Office (PNF) based on a tip-off from Swiss authorities, the PNF confirmed to OCCRP on Wednesday.

Brothers Ahmed Ali Saleh, 54, and Khaled Ali Saleh, 39, are accused of laundering proceeds from corruption and laundering embezzled public funds as part of an organized criminal group. Both men are being tried in absentia and are believed to be residing in Dubai.

Their father, Ali Abdullah Saleh, ruled Yemen for 33 years until his ouster during the Arab Spring in 2012. The former president was accused of plundering billions in state funds throughout his long tenure to enrich his family and inner circle. He was killed by Houthi rebels in 2017.

title: From Fugitive to Federal Custody: Inside the Takedown of South America’s ‘King of the South’
content:
When federal agents reached out to Sebastián Marset through his girlfriend in March 2025 to persuade him to surrender, the Uruguayan drug lord who styled himself the “King of the South” mocked them, boasting that he was "smarter than the entire D.E.A. put together."

“I’m not going to surrender,” Marset declared, according to court records. “I’ll be a criminal for the rest of my life.”

Almost a year later, heavily armed Bolivian special forces raided a residential neighborhood in Santa Cruz in the pre-dawn hours, capturing the fugitive who had evaded international law enforcement for years.

By that evening, one of the most powerful drug barons in South America’s Southern Cone - wanted by federal prosecutors for laundering millions of dollars in illicit proceeds through American banks - landed on U.S. soil in handcuffs.

Now held in a federal detention center in Virginia, Marset is mounting an aggressive legal defense. A new series of court filings has laid bare a detailed record of his global operations, missing evidence, and his own cynical view of regional law enforcement.

title: Azerbaijan Pardons French Citizen as EU Lifts Sanctions on Russian Billionaire
content:
President Ilham Aliyev of Azerbaijan pardoned 20 prisoners on Wednesday, including a French national jailed on espionage charges, shortly after the European Union removed Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov from its sanctions list.

Among those granted clemency under Aliyev’s decree was Martin Ryan, a French citizen arrested in late 2023 and sentenced by an Azerbaijani court in March to 10 years in prison.

The pardons followed a broader diplomatic deal struck after France lobbied for Usmanov's delisting. The E.U. Council announced Tuesday that it had also lifted sanctions against Mikhail Fridman, a Russia-connected businessman, while extending restrictions—including travel bans and asset freezes—on roughly 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years in response to the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine.

title: US Charges Russian Network in Alleged European Sabotage, US Murder Plot
content:
A newly unsealed U.S. federal indictment reveals that a Russian intelligence network allegedly orchestrated a targeted attack in Prague in June 2024, part of a sprawling, Kremlin-backed assassination and sabotage campaign across Europe and the United States.

The indictment’s details align directly with a known physical attack from June 2024, when a Spanish-speaking South American national was arrested for attempting to set fire to a Prague public transport bus depot. At the time, Czech Prime Minister Petr Fiala explicitly linked the incident to Moscow, stating on social media: "The unsuccessful arson attack on the buses of the Prague transport company was likely organized and financed by Russia."

Despite the U.S. charges identifying the handlers behind that attack, local law enforcement’s response remains guarded. Colonel Ondřej Moravčík, spokesman for the Czech Police Presidium, told OCCRP police are not conducting any proceedings directly related to the U.S. case and have not implemented new measures.

Spokeswoman for the Czech Interior Ministry, Ivana Nguyenová, declined to address the U.S. investigation, noting only that security services continuously monitor unusual activity.

title: UK Freezes $72-Million London Townhouse in Connection to Sanctioned Prince Group Associate
content:
British authorities have frozen a $72-million property in London in connection to an alleged associate of the Prince Group, the sanctioned Cambodian conglomerate accused of operating cyber-fraud compounds staffed in part by trafficked workers. 

Documents from the U.K. Land Registry show that a woman named Zhao Chen purchased the central London property in October 2023 for 53 million pounds ($72 million). The townhouse on a private estate in the upscale neighborhood of Belgravia features a private swimming pool and spas, according to promotional material.

British authorities placed a freeze order on the property late last month, according to the official filings obtained by Transparency International and shared with OCCRP. 

The filings show that the order was made due to Zhao Chen's association with Wu An Ming, who the U.K. has designated “an asset freeze target.” The filings do not provide information about his relationship with Zhao Chen, but OCCRP found they were married.

Official documents from the Cyprus Ministry of Interior confirm that they obtained citizenship in the Mediterranean nation together in 2018 as husband and wife.

title: Independent Journalism Is Critical For European Resilience
content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen delivered the EU’s annual state of the union address on Wednesday, calling for the robust defense of European values and warning of the dangers of cognitive warfare, foreign propaganda, and disinformation powered by viral deepfakes. 

Shaped by social media algorithms and surging AI, the integrity of Europe’s information space has become a core security and economic concern as foreign adversaries and extremists seek to paralyze democracies. Von der Leyen promised to respond by toughening sanctions enforcement and putting more funds towards promoting the rule of law. 

Europe is right to treat these issues as a high-stakes, generation-defining challenge. But there was a key omission in her speech: Independent journalism is a precondition for democratic resilience, and supporting it must remain a priority for the EU. Journalism exposes the inner workings of the threats facing our institutions, and populates our public spaces with reliable, factual, nuanced information. It is the most durable answer Europe has to the disinformation and foreign interference the President warned against. Only an informed public can make free choices.

title: How to Track Down People Who Don't Want to Be Found
content:
Whether digging into a corrupt official or trying to unmask the owner of a shady shell company, investigating a person often starts with just a handful of clues.

You may have an old phone number, a name, or a face in the background of a social media post. Taking those scattered breadcrumbs and building them into a full dossier on an individual takes a systematic approach, and is all part of a day's work for the investigative researchers at OCCRP who support journalists across the network. 

This playbook lays out the basic methods, databases, and digital tricks our team uses to track down people who don’t want to be found. No matter what kind of story you're digging into, these steps will help you safely and effectively build a profile of whoever you're looking for. 

Before diving into a digital people-search, a word of warning: setting up basic security measures is essential to protect yourself.

title: Ex-French Justice Minister Stands Trial Over Renault-Nissan Consultancy Case
content:
Criminal proceedings began Wednesday against Rachida Dati, France's former Minister of Justice and Minister of Culture, and currently the mayor of a Paris arrondissement over corruption allegations stemming from her alleged lobbying work for the Renault-Nissan car making group. 

Prosecutors accuse Dati of receiving 900,000 euros (over $1 million) between 2010 and 2012 for providing consulting services to a Dutch subsidiary of Renault-Nissan without actually performing any work, all while serving as a Member of the European Parliament and working as an attorney.

The former minister will stand trial for receiving the proceeds of abuse of authority and breach of trust, as well as for corruption and passive trading in influence committed by a person holding a public elective mandate within an international organization, the European Parliament.

She stands trial alongside co-defendant Carlos Ghosn, the former CEO of Renault-Nissan. Ghosn faces charges including abuse of corporate assets, breach of trust, corruption, and active trading in influence.

title: Instead of Helping Ukraine’s Poor, Ferrexpo’s Charitable Donations Flowed to Companies Associated With Its Then-CEO
content:
In 2017, the mining giant Ferrexpo announced it had donated more than two percent of its annual revenue to a charity based near the company’s vast iron ore mines in central Ukraine. 

This charitable spending significantly outstripped the average of its industry peers, the London Stock Exchange-listed firm highlighted in an annual report. 

Yet just one year later, questions set in. 

Auditors from Deloitte noted in Ferrexpo’s 2018 annual report that they had been unable to conclude whether the charity, named Blooming Land, had in fact spent $33.5 million of Ferrexpo’s donations on charitable ends.

Ferrexpo halted donations to the charity, which it said had been set up to “independently” coordinate the firm’s corporate social responsibility spending, and commissioned an investigation into the matter.

But the results were inconclusive: an investigating committee said only that the funds “could have been misappropriated,” and that it was unable to determine the fate of the firm’s donations.

title: Lithuanian Authorities Target Founders of Failed Cryptobank
content:
Lithuanian law enforcement authorities have formally named three co-founders of the cryptocurrency project Bankera as suspects in a criminal investigation, accusing them of siphoning off at least 45 million euro ($49 million) in investor funds following one of Europe’s largest digital token sales.

The move by Lithuania’s Financial Crime Investigation Service (FCIS) marks a major escalation in a yearlong probe stemming from investigative reporting by local news outlet 15min and OCCRP. Authorities confirmed that formal notices of suspicion were issued to the founders—Mantas Mockevičius, Vytautas Karalevičius and Justas Dobiliauskas—for the unlawful dissipation of high-value assets. All three have been requested to appear for questioning but they have reportedly left the country and apparently settled in Monaco. Their lawyer has not responded to reporter's request for comment.

title: 'Flamingo Revolution' Mounts Direct Threat to Albania's Edi Rama
content:
What began as a localized environmental campaign against a luxury resort development backed by Jared Kushner has hardened into a 100-day siege of Albania’s political center, mounting the most formidable challenge in years to the government of Prime Minister Edi Rama.

Demonstrators marched along Tirana’s main thoroughfares, rallying near local high schools to mobilize students into the movement, dubbed by organizers as the “Flamingo Revolution” as flamingos inhabit the protected Vjosa-Narta wetland ecosystem where the resort was supposed to be built. Chanting “Rama, resign” and “Your time is up,” protesters confronted security forces in the latest escalation of a campaign that has repeatedly paralyzed parts of the capital.

The unrest originally erupted over government plans to allow Kushner’s firm, Affinity Partners, to construct high-end tourism facilities on the uninhabited Sazan Island and within the protected Vjosa-Narta wetland along the Adriatic coast. While Rama framed the investment as a key catalyst for tourism and European Union integration, environmentalists fiercely opposed the privatization of pristine reserves.

title: The Son of Ljubljana’s Mayor Granted Serbian Citizenship in “National Interest”
content:
Serbian authorities granted citizenship to the son of Ljubljana’s mayor under a discreet "national interest" provision while declining to publicise the justification of its decision. The move coincides with high-value real estate purchases in the Slovenian capital by a key ally of the Serbian president, a businessman at whose Belgrade villa the mayor's son registered his official residence.

According to official records obtained by investigative news outlets Oštro and KRIK, Jure Janković - son of long-serving Ljubljana Mayor Zoran Janković - was naturalized as a Serbian citizen in November 2024. Land registry documents show that the younger Janković registered his Belgrade address at a luxury villa owned by Nikola Petrović, a powerful energy executive known widely as the "best man" and close confidant of Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić.

title: Citing Trump Crypto Fortune, US Democrats Try to Derail Bill to Regulate Digital Assets
content:
Congressional Democrats are using the sudden surge in crypto wealth accumulated by U.S. President Donald Trump as a rallying cry to defeat legislation that would create a new regulatory landscape for the digital currency industry.

The Senate is scheduled to take a procedural vote Tuesday on the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, which if passed by both legislative chambers would set new rules to govern the growing crypto sector. The procedural vote is needed for the Senate to debate the measure.

In a bid to peel off some Democrats, Republican Party leaders in Congress over the weekend incorporated ethics provisions that would prevent any U.S. president or other government officials from issuing digital assets.

“It purports to prevent conflicts of interest and corruption by the president of the United States. It is a charade. It is a sham. It should prompt a no vote by every member of the United States Senate,” said Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat.

title: Probe Into Serbian Ruling Party’s Election Call Center Yields No Progress After Three Years
content:
As Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic’s party gears up for elections at the end of October, suspicions of vote-buying in previous election cycles remain unresolved.

Serbian police have failed to question a single person in nearly three years of investigating an alleged vote-buying and illicit campaign finance scheme operated by the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), opting instead to transfer the case between internal departments, the Center for Investigative Journalism of Serbia (CINS) reported.

The stalled investigation takes on renewed significance as Serbia gears up for snap parliamentary elections on October 25. The political stakes were elevated further Monday evening when President Aleksandar Vučić announced on Pink TV that he will officially resign on September 27. Vučić stated he will address the nation to thank them for their support before entering the campaign as an “ordinary citizen” representing the SNS.

“The only thing I can say is that I faithfully served the citizens of this country, faithfully, diligently, devotedly, and with determination,” Vučić said.
snippet: As Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic’s party gears up for elections at the end of October, suspicions of vote-buying in previous election cycles remain unresolved.

title: Ghana Arrests Three for Allegedly Aiding Dutch Fugitive Drug Lord Jos Leijdekkers
content:
Authorities in Ghana have arrested three men suspected of operating on behalf of Joseph “Chubby Jos” Leijdekkers, one of Europe’s most wanted cocaine kingpins, following a massive drug seizure at a French port.

The operation, conducted by Ghana’s Narcotics Control Commission, came days after French customs officials intercepted approximately 3.9 tonnes of cocaine - valued at an estimated 225 million euro ($261 million) - at the port of Dunkirk, according to Reuters. Leijdekkers’s lawyers, Jan-Hein Kuijpers and Guy Weski, have stated in a response to Dutch media NU.nl that their client denies any involvement with the seized cocaine.

Ghanaian officials said the three suspects were allegedly assisting Leijdekkers’ network as it uses West Africa to route South American narcotics into European markets.

title: Under Cloud of Scandal, Outgoing Ukrainian Prosecutor General Targets Anti-Corruption Chief
content:
Ukraine’s outgoing prosecutor general signed a notice of suspicion Monday targeting the chief of the national anti-corruption agency, accusing him of forging documents for massive financial gain and orchestrating a sham adoption to evade prosecution.

The Prosecutor General, Ruslan Kravchenko, announced in a video statement posted on Telegram that he had formally signed charges against Semen Kryvonos, director of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU). The move ignited a high-stakes feud among top law enforcement bodies just as Kravchenko left office under a cloud of scandal. Local meda reported that he has left Ukraine.

Kravchenko also broadened his offensive to target a close associate of Oleksandr Klymenko, head of the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO). Without naming the individual, Kravchenko alleged they had attempted to bribe and influence the chief judge of the High Anti-Corruption Court while assisting someone in evading military mobilization.

title: Two Shot, Several Arrested in Clashes Over Papua New Guinea Mine
content:
At least two people were shot and several arrested in the Papua New Guinea island of Bougainville on Sunday after unknown people set fire to equipment belonging to an Indian company poised to reopen one of the world’s largest untapped copper and gold reserves.

The arson attack targeted a mining camp belonging to Lloyds Metals and Energy Ltd, an Indian company that was controversially chosen by Bougainville President Ishmael Toroama to reopen the long-shuttered Panguna mine, which is estimated to hold $160 billion in precious metals.

The attack, which sparked a shootout and retaliation, came three weeks after an OCCRP investigation raised questions about Toroama’s decision to choose Lloyds.

The investigation revealed that Toroama had signed a memorandum of understanding with Lloyds shortly after accepting an offer from its managing director for the president’s wife to travel to India and have a life-saving kidney operation at no cost.

It also quoted an expert and some locals warning that anger over the Indian company’s involvement could erupt into violence.

title: Philippine President's Cousin to be Transferred from Hospital to Jail
content:
The Philippines’ anti-graft court on Monday ordered the transfer of Martin Romualdez, former House Speaker and cousin of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., from a hospital to a regular jail a week after his arrest, OCCRP partner Rappler reported. Romualdez is accused of plunder in a 7.44-billion-peso ($118 million) case.

The transfer order follows a medical report from the Philippine General Hospital (PGH) concluding that Romualdez is clinically stable and no longer requires hospitalization. He will be moved to the New Quezon City Jail, where he will be detained while hearings on his plunder charge are conducted.

Prosecutors allege that, between 2022 and 2025, Romualdez and his co-defendants amassed billions of pesos through commissions, kickbacks and bribes from contractors and other entities seeking government infrastructure work.

title: UK Fraud Trial Opens Over $119M Car Investment Scheme
content:
Two businessmen accused of defrauding investors through a car investment scheme involving about 88 million pounds ($119 million) are due to stand trial in London, the U.K. Serious Fraud Office (SFO) said. Reginald Larry-Cole and Scott Martin each face three counts of fraud over their roles at the Raedex Consortium, which operated investment schemes including Buy2Let Cars, PayGo Cars, Wheels4Sure and Rent2Own Cars. Both men have pleaded not guilty.

Prosecutors allege the companies offered investors returns from fleets of vehicles leased to customers but ultimately collapsed into administration in 2021, leaving hundreds of investors facing losses. The SFO opened a criminal investigation that year and later charged Larry-Cole, the consortium’s founder, and Martin, its former chief executive. The agency alleges the pair made false representations to investors about the financial health and operation of the businesses between 2012 and 2021. Their trial is scheduled to begin at Southwark Crown Court.

title: Cypriot Police Seize 126 Kilos of Ketamine in Limassol Raid
content:
Cypriot police said they seized over 126 kilograms of ketamine and arrested four suspects during a coordinated raid on two residences in Limassol. Greek media claim that the operation netted two couples—one Israeli and one Palestinian. The Limassol District Court subsequently ordered all four individuals remanded in custody for eight days as officers from the Drug Enforcement Unit (YKAN) continued with the investigation.

According to official police reports, officers conducted two days of surveillance before executing search warrants on the properties. At one residence, officers discovered 126.6 kilograms of ketamine, precision scales, and mobile phones. A search at the second residence yielded smaller quantities of cocaine, ketamine, mephedrone, and MDMA, alongside untaxed cigarettes and cash in euros, U.S. dollars, and Israeli shekels.

title: Jailed Editor, Closed Outlet: The Rapid Demise of Kazakhstan’s Top Independent News Site
content:
Orda.kz, one of Kazakhstan’s leading independent news outlets, ceased publication a month after an Almaty court sentenced its editor-in-chief to eight years in prison. Press freedom advocates described the closure as the final step in a months-long state campaign aimed at silencing critical journalism.

The outlet’s majority owner, Maksat Ganiyev, publicly attributed the shutdown to financial losses, telling reporters that six years of investment had failed to yield commercial viability and denying that the decision was driven by political pressure. He described the outlet as a business project. “It has to deliver a certain return. It has to be commercially viable and interesting”, he told OCCRP.

Yet media watchdogs and legal experts view the shuttering as part of a wider, systematic tightening of state control over independent media following the adoption of a new constitution and the election of a single-chamber parliament, the Kurultai, dominated by the ruling Adilet party.

title: Timber Giant Accused of Forging Environmental Records to Hide Toxic Emissions
content:
Romanian prosecutors have charged two subsidiaries of Kronospan, one of the world’s largest producers of wood-based panels, with venting carcinogenic gases into residential areas and falsifying environmental records to conceal the pollution.

The indictment, sent to trial following a two-year investigation, targets Kronospan Trading and Kronochem, along with two company employees tasked with environmental oversight. Authorities accuse the firms of releasing nitrogen oxides and formaldehyde - hazardous chemicals used in timber processing - at levels up to three times the legal threshold between 2022 and 2023.

According to prosecutors, the industrial giant maintained the illusion of regulatory compliance through fraud. Whenever internal monitoring registered illegal pollution spikes, staff allegedly withheld the findings and repeated testing until favorable numbers were achieved.

title: Inside the Collapse of a Surrogacy Agency That Cost Surrogates and Hopeful Parents Their Dreams and Money
content:
The promise was a seamless journey towards building a family. 

Advertising services across Ukraine, Albania, Georgia, Cyprus, and Mexico, the commercial surrogacy agency World Center of Baby presented itself as a one-stop shop that would help match hopeful parents with surrogates and coordinate complex medical and legal processes. 

Some of the agency’s surrogacy packages were priced at more than $100,000.

But in February 2026, the agency sent an email to prospective parents announcing that it was declaring bankruptcy in the U.S., where its apparent main corporate entity was registered in Florida as World Center Group Corp.

The announcement triggered chaos. Online forums lit up with intended parents looking for help, saying they had been abandoned by the agency, sometimes in the midst of their surrogacy process. Reporters spoke with six couples and two single intended fathers who said they had incurred financial losses ranging into tens of thousands of dollars. For some, that spelled the end of their dream of becoming a parent.

Meanwhile, surrogates either in the midst of fertility treatments or already pregnant were left unpaid and unsupported.
snippet: The promise was a seamless journey towards building a family.
creator: Ambra Montanari, Beatrice Petrella, Mariia Horban (NGL.media), Kevin G. Hall (OCCRP), Xhesika Tollia (Shteg.org), Kelly Bloss (OCCRP)

title: Ousted Bangladesh PM's Daughter Steps Down as WHO Regional Chief after Fraud Probe
content:
Saima Wazed, the daughter of ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, resigned on Wednesday as the World Health Organization’s Southeast Asia regional director following internal fraud probes that left her unpaid for over a year.

In an emailed statement to OCCRP, Wazed confirmed she had submitted her resignation, maintaining she has been “cleared of any financial fraud charges” and possesses evidence to prove it.

“Now that the investigation has been completed, I have decided to resign and move on. I need to work and return to giving my services to the world,” she said.

The 53-year-old, who assumed the regional director role in January 2024, was investigated by the U.N. health agency over allegations of financial fraud and misrepresenting her academic credentials during her post campaign.

According to a report by independent outlet Health Policy Watch, The WHO launched its probe after Bangladesh’s Anti-Corruption Commission filed two cases against her alleging fraud, forgery, and misuse of power. It found that found the allegations were unsubstantiated.

title: Australia Charges Accountants in Multimillion-Dollar Loan Fraud Scheme
content:
Australian police have charged three accountants for allegedly helping an organized crime syndicate obtain tens of millions of dollars in fraudulent loans, bringing the total number of people charged in the probe to 33, New South Wales Police said on Thursday.

Investigators said the syndicate initially used stolen identities to finance nonexistent luxury "ghost cars" before expanding into large-scale personal, business, and home-loan fraud targeting multiple financial institutions.

Police allege the accountants misused their positions to facilitate and approve false applications. A 46-year-old accounting firm director was charged over fraudulent documents linked to $16.2 million in loans, while two others, aged 34 and 28, face charges related to $15.6 million and $14.5 million in loans, respectively.

The investigation, launched in 2024, involves state police, the NSW Crime Commission, tax authorities, and financial regulators.

title: Armenia Unveils Raid Footage in Ex-Tax Chief Probe
content:
Armenian authorities released video footage on Wednesday showing seized valuables, including paintings, firearms, medals, and jewelry, following a search at the home of former Finance Minister Gagik Khachatryan as part of an expanding corruption investigation.

Khachatryan, 71, who headed Armenia's tax agency from 2008 to 2014 and served as finance minister until 2016, was arrested last week and placed in pre-trial detention. On Sept. 1, prosecutors detailed new charges against him, alleging he accepted real estate bribes worth $5.99 million for his sons, embezzled nearly $480,000 in state funds, and laundered illicit proceeds. In a statement sent to local media, his legal team denies all accusations.

Separately, anti-corruption prosecutors are seeking to confiscate 193 properties, 14 vehicles, stakes in 29 companies, and over $48 million in cash from Khachatryan and his relatives. The actions follow a joint operation with the U.S. Department of Justice, which resulted in the January auction of Khachatryan’s $36 million California mansion, with 85% of net proceeds designated for return to the Armenian government.

title: Turkey Detains 24 in Belgium-Linked Drug Trafficking Probe
content:
Turkish authorities have detained 24 people and seized assets worth approximately $20.6 million in an operation targeting an international drug trafficking network allegedly directed from Belgium, the Justice Ministry said.

The Izmir Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office issued detention warrants for 38 suspects. Eleven of the individuals are believed to be abroad, one is already incarcerated, and police are searching for two remaining suspects.

Authorities seized 87 properties, 18 vehicles, four private boats, stakes in 14 companies, and bank accounts suspected of representing crime proceeds.

Prosecutors did not disclose the identities of the suspects, the specific types or quantities of drugs involved, or other countries where the syndicate operated. Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said investigators are targeting both the syndicate's members and the corporate vehicles used to launder illicit funds.

title: Philippine Ex-Speaker Arrested in $118M Plunder Case
content:
Former Philippine House Speaker Martin Romualdez, a cousin of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., was arrested Monday after the country’s anti-graft court issued a warrant in a 7.44-billion-peso ($118 million) plunder case involving alleged kickbacks from government flood-control and other infrastructure projects.

The Philippines’ Office of the Ombudsman filed the case against Romualdez and three other defendants: former lawmaker Zaldy Co, Romualdez’s personal assistant Joselyn Tragua Serenio, and foreign exchange company president Felicito Cristobal Guevarra. The Sandiganbayan anti-graft court subsequently found probable cause and issued arrest warrants for all four, with no bail recommended.

Prosecutors allege that between 2022 and 2025, Romualdez and his co-defendants accumulated billions of pesos through commissions, kickbacks, and bribes from contractors and other entities seeking government infrastructure work. The allegations center particularly on flood-control projects, which have become the subject of a wider corruption investigation in the Philippines.

title: Spanish Police Dismantle 'Dubai Bank' Narco-Network, Arrest 21
content:
Spanish authorities dismantled an international cocaine and money laundering network tied to a shadow financial system known as the "Dubai Bank," arresting 21 people worldwide and identifying 20 million euros ($23.24 million) in illicit assets, the National Police announced Tuesday.

The massive operation targeted what police described as the “aces” of global drug trafficking, including the capture of a high-value Europol target who allegedly led the Dubai-based narco-bank. Investigators said the illicit structure allowed criminal organizations to rapidly move funds across different countries to finance narcotics shipments.

Coordinated by the Special Anti-Drug Prosecutor's Office of the National Court, the investigation began in February 2021 after authorities intercepted the Nehir, a ship carrying cocaine from South America, off the Spanish coast. Officers arrested the nine-member crew and seized 1,835 kilograms of cocaine, but the vessel's captain deliberately caused a leak.

title: Former Swiss Banker Handed Suspended Two-Year Sentence for Corruption
content:
A Swiss court has handed Pierre Mirabaud, a former president of the Swiss Bankers Association and former partner at the private bank Mirabaud & Cie, a two-year suspended prison sentence after finding him guilty of foreign bribery and money laundering.

The Swiss Federal Criminal Court delivered its verdict late Tuesday morning, state broadcaster SRF reported.

According to the indictment, the 78-year-old former banker "continuously and systematically" funneled nearly 300 payments totaling 82.3 million Swiss francs ($101.7 million) to a senior Kuwaiti government official between 2000 and 2012. In exchange, the Kuwaiti official allegedly invested $595.2 million with the Geneva-based private bank.

Mirabaud, who chaired the Swiss Bankers Association from 2003 to 2009, pleaded guilty to making the illicit payments and admitted to his role in the corruption and money-laundering scheme.

During the hearing, Mirabaud expressed remorse. “I am here to take responsibility; that's why I accepted this procedure,” he said, according to public broadcaster RTS.

title: Murder For Hire: Details Emerge About Alleged Cross-Border Plot to Kill Twin Brothers in Cyprus
content:
On the evening of August 10, a person using the handle “Sponge Jobb” posted a call for a hitman to a group on the Signal messaging app. 

The group member, who used an avatar of the cartoon character SpongeBob SquarePants, said weapons and transport were available. The person ultimately offered $60,000 in cryptocurrency for the murder.

Days after the advertisement for a contract killer appeared, a Danish man answered. But the would-be hitman was actually an undercover officer. His work triggered an international police operation leading to an attempted murder case now unfolding in Cyprus, where the hit was allegedly intended to take place.

Those are some of the details gathered by OCCRP member center CIReN from the Cypriot court, where authorities have submitted information from their investigation into the alleged murder plot.

Many questions remain, and authorities are keeping tight-lipped as the investigation is ongoing. The targets were described in the Cyprus court only as twin brothers vacationing on the island. The possible motive for their murder has not been revealed.

title: Ecuador Convicts 15 People, 5 Companies in $398 Million Drug Money Case
content:
An Ecuadorian court has convicted 15 people and five companies for laundering nearly $398 million linked to international drug trafficking, the country’s Prosecutor General’s Office announced.

Fourteen of the defendants, including Roberto Carlos Álvarez Vera, an alleged ringleader known as “El Gerente,” were sentenced to 13 years in prison, while another received a 10-year term. The court also ordered the five companies dissolved and their assets confiscated.

Prosecutors said the network used shell companies and commercial fronts between 2015 and 2025 to wash illicit drug money through Ecuador’s financial system. Investigators traced suspicious cash and check deposits, international wire transfers, and bank loans, as well as purchases of real estate, vehicles, and livestock.

Several members of the ring had prior convictions in separate international drug trafficking and organized crime cases.

title: Ecstasy Bust in Malaysia Leaves Alleged Syndicate Boss Dead
content:
Malaysian police dismantled a drug syndicate and seized $6.79 million worth of MDMA, commonly known as ecstasy, following a raid on a makeshift laboratory that left the group’s alleged ringleader dead.

Officers recovered more than 180 kilograms of MDMA from a house converted into a processing lab for domestic and international distribution, according to state news agency Bernama.

During the operation, police shot and killed the 52-year-old suspect after he opened fire on the raiding team, said Hussein Omar Khan, director of the Narcotics Criminal Investigation Department.

Hussein added that the syndicate routinely operated out of secluded residential areas to mask its drug processing and distribution network from law enforcement.

title: Police Tapes Show Malta Businessman Acquitted of Journalist's Murder Said He Initially Approved the Plot
content:
The Times of Malta has released the full recordings of businessman Yorgen Fenech’s 2019 police interrogations in which he states that he gave the "OK" to the plot to murder investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia. He told police he then gave instructions to “stop everything.”

Caruana Galizia was killed at age 53 in a car bomb on October 16, 2017, as she drove away from her home. 

The tapes were played for the nine-member jury that on September 2 acquitted Fenech of complicity in the murder, as well as criminal association. The verdict, decided by an 8-1 vote after about eight hours of deliberation, closed a 55-day trial that exposed a web of contacts between the defendant and Malta’s political elite.

In the 2019 recordings, Fenech admitted to greenlighting the plot with middleman Melvin Theuma. He said Theuma told him his “share” of the cost to carry out the murder would be 120,000 euros, although he did not tell police he paid that amount. He did state that he paid 50,000 euros in an attempt to call off the plot three days after he had approved it. 

Theuma was granted immunity from prosecution in exchange for his testimony in the case.

title: Hungarian Media Tycoon’s Firm Formed Dubai Subsidiary While Under Investigation at Home
content:
Hungarian media tycoon Gyula Balásy broke down in tears in a May television interview, stating authorities had frozen the accounts of his companies, which had received lucrative public relations contracts under the administration of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. 

Following that admission, the National Investigation Bureau of the Emergency Police released a statement about its investigation into “suspicion of fraudulent misrepresentation in connection with overpriced contracts.” The investigation involves the National Tax and Customs Administration, and has been active since at least April in 2024.

Corporate records obtained by OCCRP and Átlátszó reveal that one of the companies that had its accounts frozen created an offshore firm in 2024, as the investigation was ongoing.

In October 2024, the records show, Balásy’s New Land Media formed a subsidiary in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) city of Dubai. 

Balásy also owns a luxury apartment in Dubai, according to property records.

title: Lack of Oversight Fuels Power Sector Corruption, Iraqi Lawmaker Says
content:
An Iraqi lawmaker has blamed a systemic lack of public procurement oversight for widespread corruption in the country's electricity contracts, revealing that parliament is drafting new legislation to bridge the regulatory gap.

Speaking to OCCRP, Taha Al-Difai, head of the Iraqi Parliament's Integrity Committee, said the absence of government oversight on public energy contracts allowed violations to proliferate unchecked.

“In the past, there was oversight provided by inspectors' offices, but currently, such oversight is absent… contracting procedures proceed easily without supervision,” Al-Difai said.

He noted that the Federal Board of Supreme Audit currently reviews contracts only after they have been signed. To resolve the issue, Al-Difai said parliament plans to enact an “internal oversight” law allowing contracts to be audited prior to signing. The draft is scheduled for a first reading next week.

He also called for amendments to Iraq’s financial disclosure rules to broaden scrutiny over the sources of public officials’ wealth and property.

title: Bosnian Police Intercept 96 Migrants, Identify Two Suspected Smugglers
content:
Bosnia and Herzegovina's border police prevented 96 people from illegally crossing the country's border, the agency said in a statement Thursday.

The smuggling attempts were thwarted in two separate operations Wednesday in the town of Bistrica. During the afternoon, officers intercepted 63 people—40 from Pakistan and 23 from Bangladesh. Acting on orders from the state prosecutor’s office, investigators seized two boats and identified two suspected smugglers.

Later that evening, authorities intercepted another 33 people in the same town, including 18 from Afghanistan, 13 from Bangladesh and two from Pakistan. Police said the country's Service for Foreigners' Affairs was notified and the investigation remains ongoing.

title: Businessman Acquitted of Commissioning Murder of Maltese Journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia
content:
Nine years after investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed by a car bomb outside her home in Malta, businessman Yorgen Fenech has been found not guilty of complicity for allegedly masterminding her assassination.

The nine-member jury returned its verdict on the evening of September 2 after about eight hours of deliberation, voting 8-1 on the charge of complicity and 8-1 on the other charge he faced for alleged criminal association. 

The verdict at the Law Courts in Valletta, Malta's capital, closes what has been one of the longest jury trials in the country’s history, running to 55 sitting days since it opened on July 1.

Fenech, 44, the former chief executive of the Tumas Group, had pleaded not guilty. 

The prosecution, led by Anthony Vella and Godwin Cini, is expected to appeal the verdict. It argued that Fenech commissioned and financed the killing, paying self-confessed middleman Melvin Theuma 150,000 euros ($ 170,000) to engage the hitmen, and that he passed Theuma information about the police investigation in the two years that followed. Theuma was granted a presidential pardon to testify in the case.

title: Ukraine Presidential Chief Responds to Alleged Laundering Role
content:
The head of Ukraine’s presidential office, has said courts should determine the significance of recordings that have raised questions about his involvement in an alleged $3.3 million money-laundering scheme aimed at securing bail for a former minister detained in a sprawling energy sector corruption probe.

Authorities have not publicly named Kyrylo Budanov and he has not been charged but  court documents obtained by the Ukrainian news outlet hromadske appear to identify him participating in a conversation concerning the money laundering.

Responding to questions about the tapes, Budanov told hromadske that any determination regarding the recordings should be made by a judge. “Let the court figure out who appears where,” he said.

title: Dutch Police Arrest 34 Following Drug-related Shootout
content:
Dutch authorities arrested 34 people Wednesday at various locations across the country following a deadly shootout in a Dutch village, reportedly linked to a notorious drug lord, public broadcaster NOS reported.

The incident unfolded around 4:00 a.m. Tuesday when dozens of masked men, several armed with heavy firearms, disembarked from two vans in Overasselt, near the German border. The group approached a farm belonging to a family allegedly involved in drug trafficking and opened fire on a car. The 51-year-old man inside the vehicle was killed, police told a press conference. The masked men also fired at two police officers, leaving one with life-threatening injuries.

title: Ukraine Busts Crypto Fraud Network Targeting EU Victims
content:
Ukraine’s Security Service and National Police dismantled a Kyiv-based crypto fraud network that allegedly targeted EU citizens and generated monthly turnover of up to $1 million at its peak. Investigators say the group, involving several dozen people and led by a 25-year-old IT specialist, posed as representatives of cryptocurrency platforms and lured victims with supposedly profitable investment opportunities promoted through Telegram channels.

After showing victims fictitious trading results, the suspects allegedly directed them to fake websites designed to mimic legitimate crypto services. The sites contained malicious “drainer” code that enabled unauthorized withdrawals once users connected their wallets and approved transactions. Police searched 23 offices and homes, seizing phones, computer equipment, cash believed to be criminal proceeds and 16 luxury cars, including Porsche, BMW and Mercedes-Benz vehicles. Authorities have not yet named any suspects, and the investigation is ongoing.

title: Spain Arrests Germany’s Most Wanted Drug Trafficker
content:
Spanish police, working with German authorities, have arrested Germany’s most wanted drug trafficker in the southern city of Málaga, the National Police announced Monday. The unnamed fugitive, detained on August 24, was wanted under a European arrest warrant for drug trafficking and organized crime, as well as a separate Spanish judicial warrant.

According to investigators, the suspect led a criminal network that used a warehouse in Spain to load large quantities of narcotics onto trucks bound for Germany via France. The fugitive, described as an expert in boxing and mixed martial arts, became the target of an intensive investigation in 2025 when authorities learned he was hiding in Spain.

To evade capture, the trafficker changed his phone number every two weeks and his identity every three months, police said, noting he had even taken a cybersecurity course in Turkey to learn how to avoid digital tracking. Following extensive surveillance, officers tracked down his brother and arrested the fugitive while he was riding in the passenger seat of his brother's car.

title: Q&A: What Has Emerged From the Trial of a Businessman Charged in the Murder of a Maltese Journalist?
content:
OCCRP: Daphne Caruana Galizia is said to have coined a phrase that has been picked up by anti-corruption activists: “Malta is not a normal country." Are there any aspects of this trial that bring the phrase to mind now that the lawyers have made their final arguments, and the jury will soon reach its verdict?

Julian Bonnici: The political shadow over the case is a long one. Keith Schembri, the former chief of staff to Malta's ex-prime minister spent close to four days in the witness box, and has been accused throughout the trial of being the real mastermind. He denies it, and little hard evidence for it has been put before the jury.

The trial has also laid out defendant Yorgen Fenech's web of contacts across Malta's political elite: his WhatsApp exchanges with Schembri, with former Prime Minister Joseph Muscat, with regulatory heads, and with the deputy police commissioner who once headed the investigation into the murder.

A lot of people know that Caruana Galizia was Malta’s most prominent investigative journalist and anti-corruption activist. Who is Yorgen Fenech, and what is the prosecution alleging motivated him to commission her murder?

title: Uganda Arrests 16 in Alleged $4M Fake Gold Scam
content:
Ugandan police have arrested 16 people, including four police officers, for their alleged involvement in a fake gold scam that defrauded a Dubai businessman of $4 million, the Uganda Police Force stated.

The suspects operated under the company name Real Sunnex Ltd and allegedly obtained the $4 million from an unnamed Dubai businessman through a fake gold transaction. According to investigators, the group was also preparing to obtain another $4 million from the businessman using a similar scheme. Investigators also said the four officers had abandoned their duties to guard the suspected fraudsters at an illegal gold refinery.

The investigation followed a complaint filed by the businessman in July 2025, in which he named Asiimwe Moses as one of the alleged fraudsters and identified the company as Real Sunnex Ltd. During the operation, police recovered fake gold, documents and eight vehicles.

title: Australia Probes Western Union Over Possible Money Laundering Risks
content:
Australia’s financial intelligence agency AUSTRAC has launched an investigation into Western Union Financial Services Australia and its U.S.-based parent company over concerns about how they manage money laundering and terrorism financing risks. The probe will examine the company’s anti-money laundering program, transaction monitoring and governance, including whether its systems can identify known laundering typologies and suspicious transactions linked to child sexual exploitation and terrorism financing.

The investigation follows previous regulatory engagement and an external audit ordered in 2025. Western Union operates one of the world’s largest international money transfer networks, including cash-based cross-border payments, a sector considered particularly vulnerable to criminal exploitation. Regulators have identified risks in the sector including fraud, human trafficking, terrorism financing and child sexual exploitation. Western Union has committed to addressing issues raised in the audit.
